title: Hamlet
author: William Shakespeare
openingChapterLabel: Act I, Scene I — Elsinore. A platform before the castle.
openingText: BERNARDO: Who's there? FRANCISCO: Nay, answer me. Stand and unfold yourself. BERNARDO: Long live the King! FRANCISCO: Bernardo? BERNARDO: He. FRANCISCO: You come most carefully upon your hour. BERNARDO: 'Tis now struck twelve. Get thee to bed, Francisco. FRANCISCO: For this relief much thanks. 'Tis bitter cold, and I am sick at heart.
about:
Hamlet is the story of a Danish prince who is told by his father's ghost that his uncle murdered him to take the throne — and is asked to avenge it. Hamlet spends most of the play not avenging it. He pretends to be mad, stages a play to confirm the ghost's claim, hesitates over a clear opportunity, accidentally kills the wrong man, drives the woman he loves to suicide, gets shipped to England, comes back, and kills his uncle only after his uncle's poison has already killed him.

It is the longest of Shakespeare's plays — about 4,000 lines — and the one with the most language about language. Hamlet talks more than any other character in any other Shakespeare play. The famous soliloquies — "To be or not to be," "O what a rogue and peasant slave am I," "How all occasions do inform against me" — are not interruptions of the action; they are the action. Hamlet is a man trying to decide whether to act, and the play is mostly the inside of that deciding.

Written around 1600, Hamlet sits at a hinge in Western literature. It inherits the conventions of revenge tragedy — the ghost, the play-within-a-play, the bloody final scene — and uses them to do something none of its predecessors had done: to put a recognizably modern interior life on stage. Hamlet doubts. He performs. He watches himself perform. He cannot tell whether his own grief is genuine or theatrical. The play does not resolve those questions. It is most haunting at the moments when its hero is most uncertain about what he is doing and why.

angleCards.title: Mad or performing madness?
angleCards.text: Hamlet tells Horatio he will put on an "antic disposition." But by Act IV it is less clear who is in control. Notice when his behaviour serves a strategic purpose — and when it seems to have slipped the leash.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Hamlet as a study in madness — whether his is real or performed, and what the difference tells us about sanity itself.

angleCards.title: The problem of acting under uncertainty.
angleCards.text: Everyone else in the play — Claudius, Laertes, Fortinbras — acts decisively. Hamlet thinks. The play takes his thinking seriously rather than dismissing it. Ask what he actually knows, and when.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand why Hamlet cannot act — what stops him when every other character in the play seems to know exactly what to do.

angleCards.title: Revenge vs. justice.
angleCards.text: The ghost demands Hamlet kill Claudius. But Hamlet wants more than death — he wants punishment that fits the crime, guilt that is witnessed. That distinction drives every delay in the play.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read this as a meditation on revenge versus justice — why revenge feels demanded but keeps being deferred.

angleCards.title: Thinking too much.
angleCards.text: "Thus conscience does make cowards of us all." Hamlet says it himself. But the play is not sure it agrees. Watch whether his reflectiveness is a flaw or a form of moral seriousness that the world he lives in cannot accommodate.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace the relationship between overthinking and paralysis — whether Hamlet's intelligence is his greatest asset or the thing that destroys him.

cast.name: Hamlet
cast.description: Son of the murdered king, nephew of the new king, once intimate with Ophelia, friend of Horatio. He returns from university at Wittenberg to find his father dead, his mother remarried to his uncle, and his world collapsed. He is brilliant, witty, contemptuous, grieving, and paralyzed. The play is the inside of his mind — and he is the most fully imagined human being in the English canon.

cast.name: Claudius
cast.description: Hamlet's uncle, the new king. He has murdered his brother, married his brother's widow, and taken his brother's throne. He is a competent ruler and a guilty man. The scene in which he tries to pray and finds he cannot — because he is unwilling to give up what the murder bought him — is one of the most theologically precise moments in Shakespeare. Not a cartoon villain. A man who chose.

cast.name: Gertrude
cast.description: Hamlet's mother, widow of the murdered king, now married to his murderer. The play does not reveal whether she knew. Hamlet rages at her in the closet scene; she does not deny what he says, and she does not confirm it. She loves her son. She drinks the poisoned cup at the end — Shakespeare leaves it ambiguous whether by accident or as a choice — and her death is the one Hamlet shows real grief for.

cast.name: Ophelia
cast.description: Daughter of Polonius, sister of Laertes, briefly the woman Hamlet loved. Her father uses her as bait to spy on Hamlet, and Hamlet — already half-mad, already cruel — destroys her in the "get thee to a nunnery" scene. After her father is killed by Hamlet, she goes mad herself, sings broken songs, and drowns in a stream. Her madness is the play's quietest tragedy, the one nobody notices in time.

cast.name: Polonius
cast.description: Lord Chamberlain, father of Ophelia and Laertes. A garrulous old courtier who dispenses sententious advice ("to thine own self be true") and meddles in everyone's business. Hamlet kills him by accident, stabbing through a curtain in his mother's bedroom, mistaking him for the king. His death is the moment after which the play moves from the tragedy of the mind to the tragedy of consequence — a chain of corpses follows.

cast.name: Horatio
cast.description: A scholar and Hamlet's only true confidant. He survives the play. Hamlet trusts him absolutely — "a man that fortune's buffets and rewards / Hath ta'en with equal thanks." At the end, with Hamlet dying in his arms, Horatio is the one who will live to tell the story. The play's last instruction, almost — "absent thee from felicity awhile" — is Hamlet asking Horatio not to follow him into death so the truth can be reported.

acclaim.quote: I have a smack of Hamlet myself, if I may say so.

whyItMatters.title: The Birth of the Modern Self
whyItMatters.body: Harold Bloom argued that Shakespeare invented the human as it is now understood, and Hamlet is exhibit A. Before Hamlet, characters in literature were largely consistent — Achilles is angry, Odysseus is cunning, Antigone is devoted. Hamlet contradicts himself. He doubts himself. He is one thing in soliloquy, another with Ophelia, a third with Horatio, a fourth with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern. He watches himself feel grief and wonders whether the feeling is real. That self-watching, self-doubting, self-correcting consciousness is what an inner life now means — and it begins, in literature, with this play. Almost every sustained interior monologue since (in the novel as much as in drama) is in some way working downstream of what Shakespeare did with Hamlet's mind. The first modern character is a man who cannot decide whether to act.

whyItMatters.title: Doubt as a Way of Being
whyItMatters.body: The play's central problem is not Claudius — the king is fairly easily damned by the play-within-a-play — but Hamlet's own incapacity. He has the proof. He has the opportunity. He still does not act. The play refuses to give a single explanation for that hesitation. Hamlet himself proposes several — cowardice, depression, religious scruple, philosophical caution, theatrical relish — and dismisses each. Modern readers from Coleridge to Goethe to Freud have proposed others, and the play absorbs them all. That refusal of a single answer is what keeps the play alive. Doubt is not depicted here as a flaw to be cured but as a condition to be inhabited. Hamlet matters now because his predicament — being given a clear duty and finding it impossible to discharge cleanly — is one modern readers recognize as their own. The play is the canonical literary text for the problem of acting under uncertainty.

whyItMatters.title: Language That Will Not Settle
whyItMatters.body: Hamlet is the play in which Shakespeare's language is most aware of itself. Hamlet puns relentlessly. He plays words against words, meanings against meanings, registers against registers. Polonius speaks in clichés and the play exposes them as clichés. Claudius speaks in court rhetoric and Hamlet hears the rhetoric. The play is full of moments where a single word — "seems," "fashion," "word" itself — opens up and refuses to close again. This linguistic restlessness is part of why Hamlet is endlessly quotable: "to thine own self be true," "there are more things in heaven and earth," "the lady doth protest too much," "method in his madness," "the rest is silence." Read in sequence, those quotations form a pocket-anthology of what English literature has done with language since. To read Hamlet is to read English at the moment it became fully capable of saying anything.
